title: The Most Dangerous Word In Leadership
author: Jeff Matlow
source: By Title Only on Substack, February 9, 2026
summary: Matlow names the word 'they' as the most corrosive term in organizational culture. When leaders and team members say 'they're delayed' or 'they don't get it,' they draw a line that splits the company into an 'us' and a 'them'—abdicating responsibility and denying accountability in the process. The word is dangerous not because it is imposing but because it hides in plain sight, quietly dividing teams and fostering blame. Customers notice this fragmentation immediately: when Lisa tells a client 'the tech team is working on it,' the client hears not reassurance but disunity. The deeper problem is identity: leaders who allow 'they' are refusing to build a coherent 'we.' Matlow traces how 'they' metastasizes: communication devolves into blame, collaboration declines as resentment builds, productivity crumbles, and eventually culture becomes toxic as best employees leave. The fix is not simply to swap 'they' for 'we,' but to first define who 'we' actually are—what 'we' own, stand for, and how 'we' behave when things fail. Only then does the language shift make sense. The real power emerges when leaders move from 'they' to 'we' to 'I': from blame to shared responsibility to personal ownership. 'They missed the deadline' becomes 'We missed the deadline' becomes 'I failed to communicate clearly.' This shift is where leaders grow.
points: The word 'they' is a permission slip to abdicate responsibility and deny accountability; it splits the organization into us-versus-them.
When leaders allow 'they' to persist, communication devolves, collaboration declines, resentment builds, and productivity collapses.
The fix is not to stop saying 'they' but to define 'we' first: who are we, what do we own, what do we stand for, how do we behave when things go wrong.
The real shift is from 'they' to 'we' to 'I'—from blame to shared responsibility to personal ownership and accountability.
Customers assume companies are unified; when they hear 'they,' they lose faith in the company's coherence and effectiveness.
quotes: The most dangerous word in leadership is 'they.
In the world of company culture, 'they' isn't a pronoun. It's a permission slip.
By saying 'they', you're refusing to be a part of the 'we.
When one word can destroy careers, cultures and companies, that's the word.
Customers don't give a shit about 'they'. Customers assume companies are unified.
They missed the deadline' becomes 'We missed the deadline' becomes 'I changed our requirements without clearly communicating it.
This is where personal growth—and leadership growth—happens. Right there in the middle of the 'they'.” Archived from By Title Only on April 21, 2026 by Tim.
